RX 9070
Ryzen 5600
32 GB RAM
Installed on 2TB SSD

I've only played Warzone's Casual Battle Royale (150 + bots) and I am enjoying it. However, the game has problems that do hinder the experience.

The short version is if you like COD, have a decent rig, and have friends who want to play Warzone then download and play it. Otherwise you're better off playing something else.

Good:
- Gameplay is fast
- Loads of weapons
- Challenges to do in-between shootouts
- Lots of customisation
- Vehicles speed up traversing the map
- Plenty of unique battlegrounds
- Multiple ways to respawn/revive

Cons:
- Performance is sluggish (all low settings and not getting higher than 110fps)
- Slow load times between matches and respawn states (Running on SSD)
- Map is too big
- Lots of nothing going on
- Game heavily leans on mid to long-range combat so weapons like shotguns are underwhelming
- Grenades and abilities feel useless
- Time to kill is inconsistent
- Challenges are basic 'go here' or 'wait here' missions
- Over 150GB's of storage required (even if only playing warzone)
- Extremely messy and cluttered UI
- Store is completely pointless and full of awful skins

review:
I’ve been a long-time CoD fan, especially of the Black Ops era, but the current state of the franchise is nothing short of toxic. The core gunplay still has potential, yet the entire experience is ruined by manipulative design choices that make the game feel more like a psychological trap than a fair competitive shooter.

Matchmaking Hell (SBMM/EBMM):
The game constantly throws me into lobbies where my team plays like bots while the enemy team is stacked with highly skilled players. It doesn’t matter how well I perform; the system deliberately handicaps me. Even when I carry with insane numbers or earn a Kill Chain, the outcome is already rigged by bad teammates.

Shotguns and snipers—my main weapons—become a joke. I can land a perfect point-blank shot, and it registers as a hitmarker while my opponent walks away untouched. Meanwhile, enemies melt me instantly. This isn’t bad aim—it’s intentional netcode manipulation and engagement balancing.

Despite top performance, I rarely get Play of the Game. Wins are scarce not because I underperform, but because the system keeps punishing me for doing well. After hours of grinding, maybe one match feels enjoyable, while the rest are pure frustration.

The game no longer respects player skill or time. It manipulates outcomes to keep you hooked, cycling you through loss streaks and rare “dopamine” wins. This is gambling mechanics disguised as matchmaking.

Final Verdict

CoD has become unplayable, unfair, and unethical. It’s no longer about skill or competition; it’s about being controlled by an algorithm that decides whether you’re allowed to enjoy the game.

I’m done. Like many others, I’d rather quit than continue supporting a franchise that punishes its most dedicated players.

review:
[b]Note: This is written from the perspective of someone who dabbled in Fortnite when it first came out, Warzone for a few months in 2020 and Rainbow for about a year, but aside from that has never played shooters consistently, or well. [/b]

As someone who didn't grow up liking shooters due to my severe inability to aim, this was the first time my friends convinced me to buy one and play with them. I dumped the cash and played through the single-player first.

I absolutely loved it. 
I loved the characters (though I wish they fleshed out some of their backgrounds more) and the interactive nature of the base home you stayed at. The little puzzles, the stealth, the story itself--it was all unique to me, and I appreciated just walking through some of the areas to see how far I could push the game. The gun play was forgiving, even on harder modes, which allowed me to not get frustrated or heated. And the environments were just nice to look at.

The multiplayer was a different experience, but I enjoyed practicing and seeing my aim and overall skill improve over time. I liked the guns, I appreciated that the overall lack of recoil on a lot of the guns made it hard to blame anything except my own aim. I enjoyed the struggle of being bad at games because I knew how to improve. Seeing my guns unlock cool camos and add-ons was satisfying. 

Warzone was the same as always, and it was nice when Verdansk came back, the map I originally played in. Dying to snipers sucks as always.


My main issues with this game, which is similar to most folks, is the amount of space this game takes up. Aside from that, I'm not a fan of the ridiculous skins that have come out, and the absurdity of announcing BO7 less than a year after 6's release.

[u]The Software Itself[/u]
I have had to buy a new hard drive for this game. I've personally never had a severe crash more than once or twice, but have had semi-consistent graphic bugs (probably cuz I have a GEFORCE 1080).

[u]The Skins[/u]
The skins that have come out since launch have gotten increasingly unserious, and I'm not trying to pretend that this game has to be 100% gritty and militaristic, but I refuse to accept death from the hands of Beavis and Butthead. This is a game about humans, people from military organizations. It completely rips you out of any kind of immersion, and more than that, it just looks like the cheap money grab that it is. I have a handful of skins, but at the very least they keep operators realistic, human, and wearing nothing more than a funky outfit or cool shades. 

[u]Black Ops 7[/u]
I can't say much about BO7's (personally) premature announcement other than it feeling like an absolute spit in my face after dropping so many hours and dollars on this game. Everyone knows that their efforts are going to the new game, and it won't be long until 6 is completely thrown to the side. The worst part is, I know everyone is going to buy 7 because they know that. 

Admittedly, it's sad to see a company that seemingly has a bad track record with its community and truly listening to its desires for the game. 
But, I have, and still do, enjoy this game heavily, and it is the first time I've spent this long on any mainstream game. It scratches a particular itch in my brain. So anyone that's new to this franchise, enjoy it as much as you can. Deal with the hard drive sacrifice, and have fun. 
I am planning on going back to MW1-3. I hear they're great.

At the end of the day we're all addicted and need help but hey, it is what it is.

Call of Duty (HQ) presents itself as a centralized hub for the franchise, but instead of providing convenience, it creates frustration. By forcing all entries into one bloated installation, it consumes enormous amounts of storage space unnecessarily. This approach undermines accessibility and punishes players who only wish to engage with one specific title in the series. Rather than streamlining the experience, it complicates it.
Visually, the franchise has shifted away from its signature gritty realism toward bright, cartoonish aesthetics. Skins and cosmetic packs now dominate the presentation, often resembling the style of games like Fortnite rather than maintaining Call of Duty’s military authenticity. This departure in tone alienates long-time fans and erodes the visual identity that helped define the series. Even the more detailed environments are overshadowed by the jarring, unrealistic designs of character models.
Overall, Call of Duty (HQ) is a misstep that damages the franchise’s identity, convenience, and appeal. By forcing massive installations, undermining story delivery, weakening gameplay flow, and adopting a misguided visual direction, it strips away much of what made Call of Duty unique. Instead of enhancing the player experience, it clutters and detracts from it. The result is a platform that feels unnecessary, intrusive, and disconnected from the series’ roots.
Call of Duty (HQ) gets a 1/10.

review:
This game is a finely honed dopamine dripfeed and money machine.
[b]Quality[/b] in [i]ANY[/i] element of this product outside of that core hyperfocus is utterly incidental [i]at best[/i]. 

This has been my first Call of Duty experience since Black Ops 1 (which I thought was [i]okay[/i]), and the vast majority of it has been depressingly mediocre (nvm how much has somehow gone backwards since blops1). [b]Every[/b] single 'good' moment I have had in my 1.3K+ hours spent playing Black Ops 6 / Warzone (with a tiny smidge of Zombies) would have been easily better had it occurred in another game, either by having the same gameplay situation play out, or simply by playing with the same friends. Every. Single. One. 

The UI/UX is so atrociously bad that every single person who was responsible for it being released and continuing to exist in this state should be truly, DEEPLY ashamed of themselves. 

Every single moment spent outside of an active match is a processional masterclass in "Get it done. Yesterday. Last week. No time to fix this or go back to that. Is the new thing added? Get to work on the next content update. We need to sell more. SELL MORE!", and it's an agonising, sickening shame.

Inside a match? There is some fun to be had, but frustrations and annoyances still abound.
There are so many small easy win improvements that could make the game so much more enjoyable... if only the game's purpose was to be good, rather than maximally profitable.

Whether it be the stark contrast in attention to detail between elements of the game looking to push a sale vs everything else, the CONSTANT bombardment of ads for paid content, questionable / inconsistent / incoherent balancing, the disgusting frequency of glitches/bugs ranging from trivial through annoying to outright broken, blatant aimbotters are still not uncommon despite using invasive and compatibility-breaking kernel 'anti-cheat', the server-side heuristic behavioural anti-cheat engine's high false positive rate, or any of a truckload more things besides, nothing here sparks joy. Least of all the notoriously [b]  T O X I C  [/b] playerbase, far too many of them doing their best to live up to the reputation.

Absolutely nothing makes me like, or want to play this era of COD beyond its use as a no effort zero brain distraction and dopamine grind of the FPS(/BR) variety. Such is the potency of its core game loop optimisation (nvm the predatory psychological manipulation). Well, that, and spite. Because I put in the hours to [b]know[/b] what I'm talking about in saying

[h1]This is a trash game[/h1] [h2]for trash people[/h2] [h3]or people who don't know any better[/h3].

[h2]Your time, money, and attention are better spent elsewhere[/h2]

The fact that multiple parts of the BF6 open beta were already SIGNIFICANTLY more polished than the current COD retail experience make it unlikely I'd be coming back to COD after BF6 drops, but since the majority of fps gamers I know have already said they're going to BF6 (including every new friend met through COD), that chance drops to absolutely zero.

And that sparks joy.

Unlike this game.

Do yourself all the favours:
Do ANYTHING else with your time.

And be better to one another.

Call of Duty's current state is a major disappointment and the game is dead. It's plagued by issues that seem to be pushing the player base away.

Hackers and "Sweats": The game is full of cheaters, and the constant, intense lobbies make it difficult for casual players to have fun.

Skill-Based Matchmaking (SBMM): This system has created a frustrating and seemingly unfair experience. It often feels like the game actively works against you, with lower-skilled players getting what feels like a boost to even out the playing field.

Rigged Gameplay: The flow of matches often feels manipulated. It's as if the game gives you a "mercy win" after a long losing streak to encourage you to keep playing.

Microtransactions: The focus on selling in-game items has taken priority over delivering a high-quality, balanced game.

I remember when Call of Duty was celebrated for its pure, competitive gameplay. The experience now feels rigged and focused on monetization rather than skill.

review:
Call of Duty started as a great mil-sim FPS that competed with Battlefield, Medal of Honor, America’s Army, and Arma. Today it competes against arcade shooters like Apex Legends and Fortnite. The movement is terrible. Jumping, sliding around, sliding sideways while shooting, proning out while shooting is just all way over the top. The skins, non-combat operators, are terrible. Guns that shoot bubbles and lightning bolts are terrible.

On top of that, the gameplay experience is frustrating in other ways. Skill-based matchmaking makes nearly every lobby sweaty and punishing, removing the casual fun that older CoDs were known for. Time-to-kill feels inconsistent, and weapon balance is almost always skewed toward a handful of “meta” guns while the rest of the arsenal feels useless. The store is pushed harder than the game itself, with overpriced bundles and constant cosmetic cash-grabs overshadowing the actual content. And when you finally get into a match, server issues, broken hit detection, and bugs only add to the frustration.

I think if the latest couple of CoD games were named as something different, they would do fine with whatever crowd they attract. As of now, I cannot recommend this game to anyone who expects CoD to be what CoD originally was.

review:
Call of Duty is still fun at its core. The gunplay feels tight, movement is solid, and when matches actually run smoothly, it’s some of the most addictive multiplayer you can get. But that’s where the praise ends.

The install size is absurd, 250–300GB+ for a multiplayer shooter is unacceptable. I shouldn’t have to sacrifice half my SSD just to play one mode. Updates are constant, massive, and often break more things than they fix.

SBMM makes casual play feel sweaty every game, while cheaters still slip through despite anti-cheat supposedly being 'improved.' Hit registration is inconsistent, dying behind cover is common, and servers feel unstable for a AAA title. Campaigns have been forgettable, basically glorified tutorials for Warzone.

It’s not a bad game, it’s just a bloated, mismanaged one. Strip down the file size, fix the netcode and anti-cheat, and actually listen to the community, then CoD could be great again. Until then, it’s fun for a few matches… before frustration sets back in.

Anti-cheat? Don’t make me laugh. It’s supposed to be "Ricochet," but it feels like it’s either go big or go home Valorant-style kernel-level intrusion OR absolutely nothing. Meanwhile, lobbies are a cesspool of wallhacks, aimbots, and closet cheaters who have been blatantly ruining games for months. The sheer number of cheaters is insane. I’ve played F2P garbage with better integrity.

And the player models/skins? What even is this game anymore? I signed up to play a military FPS, not Fortnite with Muppets. Cartoon operators, glow-in-the-dark skins, anime crossovers—it kills any kind of immersion. CoD used to feel like a shooter; now it’s a cash shop masquerading as one. Give me soldier models only, grounded and gritty, not whatever this clown show is supposed to be.

But the absolute cherry on top: communication bans in a rated M game. Why? It’s literally marketed as "intense violence, blood, gore, strong language." Yet somehow, me dropping a swear word or flaming a cheater is ban-worthy? It’s a joke. 

At this point, I’m convinced they don’t care about player experience at all.

Call of Duty sucks now. This series used to be all about semi realistic military pvp.  We had meaningful campaigns, and online PvP was a uniform experience.

Heck, some games didn't even give us a campaign. What happened to this franchise? 

World at War was peak. So was the original Modern Warfare trilogy.

Avoid it. The game has potential, which is what we've been saying for years, but the devs are absolute trash. Genuinely one of the worst dev teams in gaming history. I don't think it will be shutting down anytime soon since there seems to be a bit of a sunk costs fallacy at work here for AGS. The sad reality is it will most likely continue to hobble along with a few thousand concurrent players and experience a few small spikes around seasonal "content." Additionally, the dev team has no concept of balancing weapons in PVP, or no intention of doing it. I think its more likely that the idea simply exceeds their grasp. The dev team is incapable of doing this even at a core level of gameplay, like ranged vs melee. This leads to a situation where a very small handful of builds outperform literally anything else in the game, so everyone runs these builds. This is doubly true for gear perks - despite over a hundred different weapon/armor perks existing in the game, you will choose between 3 or 4 for both PVE and PVP. Nothing else is remotely viable in end game content. This fundamentally undermines what should be the most engaging combat style in any MMO.

review:
Before I start my review, I ought to give a bit of background to my playtime. I originally started playing when the game first launched in 2021 while isolating with COVID (Ahhh memories). I put roughly 40 hours in then but quickly found myself getting bored with the bugs, server issues and otherwise lack of polish/ Content. 

Fast forward to good ol' 2025. After not quite being able to scratch the MMO itch for a while, I decided to pick New World up again and even bought the DLC for good measure. This time around, My experience was drastically different. The game felt polished, Everything flows nicely. I was surprised by just how much it had changed and for the better. It finally felt like what was promised all those years ago. The trade skills are fun to level, I have yet to feel like im grinding anything out because activities such as chopping trees is actually enjoyable. This is how an MMO should be, Not taking 30 hours to gain one level.

 Now I have played A LOT of runescape over the years and my fair share of WOW but each time I go back to them I hit the same wall of the games demanding every ounce of free time I have. Luckily, New World does not have this issue. It's your casual persons MMO which is something I have been yearning for for a long time. You don't need to spend every waking hour playing it just to fit in with the playerbase. All through the levelling and questing you constantly see people at your own level which helps the feeling that you're not playing catchup to a playerbase that has spent the last 4 years no-lifing the game. There's no pressure to constantly run the best in slot gear or play a Meta setup. The playerbase on the whole is really friendly and active. 

Now with regards to the DLC, I can understand the veteran players frustrations. They've poured a lot of time into the game only to be met with a fairly expensive DLC that adds features that should have been standard in the first place. We get it, It no fairsies. I can see it from the developers side though. Yes, Amazon as a whole are worth more than most European countries. They are not, however, going to keep pumping money into the game if there's no return for them. Compare new world to other MMO's and I'd say the cost of playing is VERY cheap. one DLC in 4 years is a small price to play to maintain a game where you can lose thousands of hours. I'd happily buy a new DLC every year (which would hopefully contain more than the current one) if it meant keeping the game running and the community alive. The cosmetics store is also fairly non-intrusive. It's there if you want it but I wouldn't say it gets shoved in your face a lot.

All in all, If you find yourself getting bored of the standard run of MMO's out there, Give new world a try. Its worth its price tag for what you're getting.

review:
Came back after many, many years of not playing and having pre-ordered way back when, I felt I needed to give New World a fair shot after not having seriously played, and boy was I glad I did. The new areas, the mount system (I like it, understand why some don't though) new weapons, enemies, etc. It was all so refreshing but it still very much retained the reason I bought it in the first place: I can spend hours doing nothing but gathering or I can run mutated expeditions or I can do both, or I can go decorate my house, or I can go craft. It's all just a wonderful, play-at-your-own-pace experience. 

IMO you get your money's worth with the main story quest line alone, and that only gets you to level 65. At that point, the real end game begins with farming mutations and the crafting grind and so much more (albeit the crafting grind is annoyingly grindy even for an MMO, and absurdly expensive - please AGS) 

It's a really fun MMO experience, offering a refreshingly straightforward combat system, the ability to play whatever style you want (although another healing main hand would be great). There are definitely "meta" builds, with guides galore, but highly recommend just feeling the skill trees out yourself first. The mechanics aren't super hard to understand, even for me, which is saying a lot, and most builds, assuming you understand the general idea of what you're building, will handle most of the PVE content this game has to offer excluding the end-game stuff like Hive, M2/3's, stuff like that. You could probably be just fine not following a meta guide and cruise through M1's just fine. 

Not to mention the utterly beautiful world design and uniqeuness each area has. Riding into town on your mount and seeing people hammering down at the workbench or smelting, the little audible ambiance of it all, it's all so inviting and to be honest it feels very immersive at times. 

Season 9 just came out, and with how much proposed content AGS has for Season 10 (spoiler, it's A LOT of neat stuff: procedural expeds, endgame overhaul, more PVP modes, raids, dungeons) now is a time to test it out. If a lot of the roadmap changes do indeed come to fruition, it'll change a lot with the new season, but time will tell if that is actually the case.

I love this game. The gameplay is amazing. It has just enough sand in the box to be enjoyable and considered a sandbox. The fishing system is very nice. You even get a dedicated fishing questline that gives you really good fishing gear at the end. Everything about the game is great, except the leveling system. I don't like having my character's progression amount to nothing every expansion like in WoW just to keep things "new".

That being said, the reason I do not recommend this game is the CONSTANT CRASHING and the bugs! It is a buggy MESS of a game. From leather item icons in the crafting menu being switched, like rough leather gloves and rough leather pants icons. The fact that when you sell items to a sell order the items in the list of your items to sell does not disappear. They stay there, as though you still have the item. Which gets very confusing when you're trying to sell lots of items.

That's not even the worst of it! Most of the time, I am unable to launch the game! It literally will load the launcher then open to a black screen that eventually just stops responding forcing windows to close it. I literally have to shut down my laptop, NOT RESTART, BUT SHUT DOWN, just to launch the game. And it only launches SOMETIMES. I will literally have to shut down EVERY. SINGLE. TIME. I want to re-attempt to launch the game. And when it does actually launch, if I close the game, I ALWAYS have to shut my laptop down to try again. Not only that, but the game will randomly crash WINDOWS due to its kernel-level anti cheat software bugging out. Literally crashing to BSOD (now black screen of death) with the failure code and of course the anti-cheat as the culprit. This game is essentially MALWARE. I would love to get a refund, but unfortunately, I have 32 hours into the game and well above the time-limit on steam. And there's no actual support or a place to submit issues except in-game "feedback" that does nothing. You can't even upload screenshots of the issues you have anywhere and Amazon couldn't care less.

Also, for those considering getting the deluxe edition it is NOT worth it at all IMO. The mount looks awful, the armor skin looks awful. Unless you REALLY love the mount/armor skin, go for it. Otherwise, it is NOT at all worth it. Save your money to get a better cash shop mount/armor skin and buy the regular version instead.

My specs, for reference:
ASUS ROG Strix G18 (2024) Laptop
Intel i9 14900HX
Nvidia Gefore RTX 4080
Upgraded RAM to 64GB
2-2TB NVME SSDs

Hardware is not the issue here.

Editing my review: It seems to be an issue with DirectX12 renderer. When I set the -dx11 flag I don't get any crashing or errors. I'm not going to change my negative review until it's all fixed. This game has been out for 4 years already and there shouldn't be this many issues.

Target locking

Enhanced hit reactions

Gamepad-friendly mechanics

Aim assist for smoother controller play

review:
I don’t usually leave reviews, but after seeing so many negative ones—especially from people with over 1,000 hours of gameplay—I felt the need to speak up about how good this game actually is.
It honestly makes no sense to me how someone can sink 500+ hours (sometimes over 1,000) into a game and still leave a negative review. If a game keeps you playing that long, it's clearly doing something right.

Active Community & Ongoing Support

This game still has a large, active player base across PC, PlayStation, and Xbox. Servers are populated, and you’ll have no trouble finding groups for any activity. The devs also continue to support the game with frequent updates and seasonal events that add variety and excitement to the experience.
Content for Every Type of Player 
Whether you're into PvE, PvP, solo or group play, this game delivers:
Farming & crafting
Dungeons & raids
Guilds & large-scale PvP wars
PvP matchmaking
Rare item & cosmetic skin hunting
Player housing with actual combat benefits
A full-featured auction house where you can flip items or gear up
Elite chest runs for farming high Gear Score equipment
You're also not locked into a single playstyle. You can freely respec your stats and try out different builds whenever you want.

Not a Money Grab

One of the best things about this game is that it’s not a cash grab.
The DLC is entirely optional. Around 90% of the endgame content takes place in areas that are included in the base game. You can enjoy high-level dungeons, PvP, raids, elite runs, and more without ever buying an expansion.
No pay-to-win mechanics. All in-game purchases are purely cosmetic—and even then, you don’t need to spend money to look good. The game is filled with awesome cosmetic rewards you can earn just by playing, especially from dungeons and high-end activities.

Final Thoughts

If you’re on the fence because of the reviews, take a closer look at how many hours those players have actually spent in the game. That alone speaks volumes.
This game offers hundreds (if not thousands) of hours of content and freedom to play your way. You 100% get your money’s worth.

The new flail weapon is another standout. It’s versatile, mixing melee power with defensive and support abilities, which really shines in group play. Speaking of groups — this expansion is at its best when you team up. Whether you’re running expeditions, exploring the new Elysian Wilds zone, or just farming resources together, there’s a real sense of camaraderie.

The DLC also bumps the level cap to 65, adds Artifact gear with unique perks, and expands crafting, giving veteran players like me a reason to keep pushing forward. Sure, there are still occasional bugs and the mount unlocking questline is a bit of a grind, but these feel minor compared to the sheer amount of content and fun.

Verdict: An excellent expansion that breathes new life into the game — fast travel, richer team play, and more goals to chase. For MMO fans, especially those who loved WoW, this is absolutely worth diving into

review:
I write this review as someone who only played the base game. I have not touched the expansion or desert zone.

As much fun as I had leveling a character to 60 and maxing out the gathering and crafting professions, recommending this game would feel disingenuous. 

Pros:
The game is beautiful. The combat is fun. Gathering flowers is satisfying. Chopping down any tree in every forest is fun. Getting XP for gathering and crafting is nice. Dungeons are fun and look awesome, to the point where I had to stop several times just to take it all in. Gooning elite areas with hundreds of players to loot chests was very fun. PvP exists if that's your jam.

Cons:
The server design feels woefully outdated and singlehandedly makes me not recommend this. New World shifted from a hardcore pvp game during development, and we saw the trappings of that design at release: fully disjunct servers, each with several areas that could be conquered by factions, granting them bonuses. This system sounds cool but ultimately leads to one faction dominating every server, and as time passes and players drop off you need to inevitably merge several nearly empty servers, rendering all that work capturing areas pointless. They should have skipped this system all together and had one unified server per region, with appropriate sharding. I don't think an MMO like New World can survive unless it works just as well with 1,000 players as it does with 1,000,000 players.

The gear grind sucks. Grinding the same dungeons over and over to get slightly better gear each time is boring.

PvP not scaling properly means you have to grind max level items before you can engage with it, unless you want to be massacred.

QoL features were extremely lacking  at the point I stopped playing. Shuffling back and forth between your stash and crafting benches to craft sucked. The dungeon finder, once introduced, was a big disappointment.

Overall:
There is definitely a good game in there, but I really think the game devs were not experienced enough making MMOs. The drastic shift in focus during development, even up to release, should raise some red flags. Too much of the design of this game holds it back from being worth getting into.

review:
Bought the game at launch but came back recently. Dont listen to the majority of the haters. I was put off for so long because it seems like everyone and their mothers hate this game but after biting the bullet and reinstalling it, Ive had an experience unmatched by anything ive ever felt playing any MMORPG. I’ve played almost all the big ones having accumulated hundreds of hours on ESO, GW2, WoW and FF14 and new world has to be hands down my favorite. Shout out to the community in AP southeast for making it an even better experience than it already is.

Pros
-Best PVP ive experienced in any MMO thus far. I usually avoid PVPs in MMOs because i really hate having to reshuffle my stats and gear to not be one shotted constantly butbits different here. I took time to make a build that allows me to play all kinds of content comfortably which is not possible in other MMOs, particularly ESO. 

-Easy to understand and intuitive crafting and awesome life skilling.  I usually am not a crafter not a life skiller because i mainly enjoy doing end game PVE but gathering materials and seeing my skills go up everytime i do things like mining is just so fun in this game. Crafting gear also lets you choose your perks on armour which really helps you build your character to your liking and is a completely viable choice of getting gear (however i would like to note that crafting the best gear would require you to actually play endgame content to get the schematics for it which i understand would put off some of the people who enjoy a more casual experience.

-Incredible world design and atmosphere.  I have never enjoyed a world as much as I do in new world, the only thing that comes close to it for me personally. Every zone has a hnique atmosphere and I love that you can level up your standing in every zone passively just by exploring and doing whatever you want.

-Build diversity and variety. I really enjoy collecting artefacts and reading up  on different perks and unique items to make really awesome builds. I spend hours on end testing and theory crafting and its extremely addictive. Items like “The Abyss” or stat scalping gems allow players to play how they want. I personally love being able to play rapier and use magic and have it hit like a truck. 

-Objectively the best monetisation model in any MMO. There is absolutely nothing you can buy in the game to put yourself at an advantage over other players. Theres no way for you to buy gold, buy power or anything of that sorts, everything in the cash shop is purely cosmetic. And best part about it? No sub fee. You buy the game once and thats it, you have the full experience. Maybe a DLC will drop once in a while but thats pretty much it.  Im so sick of people defending predatory systems in MMOs and saying things like “its not pay to win but pay for convenience” its really sad that we are enabling this kind of monetisation that really has no respect for their playerbase and im really glad new world is one of the few MMOs that still have not implementing anything like this even during periods with low player retention where most other big MMO publishers would have done so.

Cons
-Dont like the speed runners who do their dailys and always queue low level dungeons. This is an aweful thing for new players because a lot of times max level players would queue a low level dungeon for a fast daily clear and the few low level players who are unfortunate enough to be queued with them would often get left behind not being able to get loot or enjoy the dungeon. Which is unfortunate because i really love the dungeons in this game.

-Toxic raiding community. Raid is achievable with a team of  non meta build players as long  as newer players somewhat know what they are doing and are not stubborn about having to change bits and pieces of their build. Unfortunately the vets would often refuse to help new players out but new players more often than not also refuse to change their builds when doing pubs  and are very stubborn. I suggest some sort of queuing system is put in place for raids that require players to have a baseline set of stats for their roles. 

-Character creation could use more sliders and options and some of the cosmetic items look really goofy. Recent ones have been awesome tho 

TLDR New World has become my home MMO and is currently my favourite game. Before any of the vets or just genuinely angry people come and say “yeah sure just give it a few thousand hours and youll run out of things to do” or “honey moon period” like im so sick of hearing this. If i ever even reach a stage where im bored of the game then just let me reach that stage naturally. I am having a good time with it so ill keep playing it. If im bored ill put it down and play something else.

review:
After nearly 900 hours in New World, I can confidently say this game is one of the most immersive MMORPGs I’ve played. The world design is breathtaking — from dense forests and eerie ruins to vibrant cities, the game’s visual atmosphere pulls you in and keeps you there. You feel in Aeternum, not just playing it.

Combat is another strong point. The action-based system rewards skill, positioning, and timing. Whether you’re in small-scale PvP or large-scale Wars and Outpost Rush, it’s fast, responsive, and genuinely fun — a rarity in the MMO space where tab-targeting often dulls the experience.

Optimisation has come a long way since launch. Performance is solid now on decent rigs, with noticeably smoother gameplay and reduced hitches or stutters. It’s clear the devs have worked hard to get the technical side under control.

That said, content has historically been New World’s weak spot. While the foundation is excellent, seasonal updates haven’t always landed with the depth or consistency players expect. Still, with the latest expansion, the game feels more complete than ever. There’s now enough PvE, PvP, crafting, and exploration content to easily push well past 1000 hours — and I’m only just getting into the new expansion.

Yes, it gets flak — and much of it is understandable — but there’s so much to enjoy here. If you love MMORPGs with immersive worlds, meaningful PvP, and visceral combat, New World delivers. It's not perfect, but it’s definitely worth your time.

review:
Here’s a balanced review of New World: Aeternum, highlighting what makes it awesome and where it falls short.

Positive Points

Aeternum’s world is gorgeous on PC, with vibrant forests, creepy swamps, and detailed environments, enhanced by dynamic lighting and high-res textures for an immersive vibe. Action-based combat feels tight with mouse and keyboard, offering diverse weapons like Greatsword and Blunderbuss for thrilling, skill-driven PvE and PvP fights. The classless system lets you swap weapons and playstyles anytime, with deep skill trees keeping builds fresh and fun for experimentation. Updated quests and cinematic cutscenes make the Azoth-driven story of the Eternal Isle more engaging and easier to follow than the original.

A streamlined early game and solo-focused content make it great for casual PC players, with co-op options for when you want to team up. Gathering resources like wood or ore is satisfying, with boosted trade skills for archetypes like Ranger, making crafting a fun part of progression. The 10-player Hive of Gorgons raid mixes exciting combat, clever puzzles, and unique gear perks, offering a solid endgame challenge.

Cross-play with consoles keeps the PC community lively, making it easy to group up for PvE expeditions or PvP battles.

Horses, wolves, and lions speed up travel, with customizable looks and upgrades, cutting down on the slog of running across Aeternum.

Amazon’s ongoing patches, seasonal events, and new gear keep it fresh and engaging for long-term players.

Negative's

Settings Limitations: There’s no option to fully hide other players’ mounts or pets, even in crowded areas. The “Hide Characters” setting (under Graphics > Visuals) only reduces player models at low FPS and doesn’t consistently hide mounts or pets, leading to visual clutter and performance dips. Despite optimizations, crowded areas like settlements or world events can cause frame drops on mid-range PCs, and high graphical settings demand a beefy rig.

While the story is improved, many side quests still feel samey, relying heavily on fetch or kill tasks, which can get tedious for players wanting more variety. Leveling up trade skills or endgame gear can feel like a slog, requiring hours of gathering or farming, which might bore players who aren’t into grinding.

The game’s systems—like territory control or crafting—can overwhelm new players, with tutorials that don’t fully explain complex mechanics.

While PvP is fun, open-world PvP requires flagging, and structured modes like Outpost Rush can have long queue times, frustrating players who love competitive play.

Peak times can lead to lag or disconnects, and server merges in the past have caused inventory or progress bugs, though patches have improved this.


Overall, No game is perfect, but it’s a ton of fun. The world is gorgeous, combat feels great, and there’s so much to do, from crafting to epic raids. The item shop’s premium currency is a pain, and settings like hiding mounts or pets don’t work as well as they should, which can make things feel cluttered or laggy. Still, if you’re down for a grind and love exploring a vibrant world, it’s a blast. The mix of solo-friendly quests, deep systems, and cross-platform play keeps you hooked, even with the hiccups.

review:
Was looking to get into a proper action-combat MMO for years, and completely missed New World.
Had some very fun few hundred hours before the gameplay loop started to get boring, but I literally couldn't stop playing for almost 3 weeks before that happened, which is why I still recommend the game.
It is very good overall, despite bugs, weird direction decisions and slow development. Also management changed couple months ago and a lot more content is expected to be released this year.

Pros:
+ Action combat system. Felt shallow in the beginning, but turned out to be of great depth eventually. Also make sure you try all weapons to get those you have fun with, don't just follow meta if you don't enjoy it.
+ Being able to change classes/builds. I didn't like the idea of not having strictly defined classes when I started, but that turned out to be an awesome part of the gameplay for me. I even bought additional build slots for convenience (you have 2 by default). Switching to a different class is very refreshing.
+ Art style and atmosphere. I just like them, and it's quite unique if you played all those copy-paste Korean MMOs for the last ~12-15 years.
+ 3v3 arena PvP mode. I only wish I could stay in the query after the match and hop onto the next one without getting back into the worlds.

Cons:
- Making money in this game is a chore, and you need a lot if you want to have a proper endgame gear.
- Same goes for the endgame raids, it's a chore even if you have properly composed build. 
- Mining basically any ores is a very miserable experience in my book: nodes are shared between all players on the server. So whenever I need to mine some to progress with the Trading Skills, try to find some nodes using nwdb.info maps or YouTube videos with routes and see empty nodes like 80% times no matter what time I do it (early morning, middle of the day, evening, at night, 3am, etc.) - I just feel like I'm being pushed for daring to mine. Very frustrating.
- Free-For-All PvP zone Artifacts quests and players who group up and farm you, preventing you from doing said quests. Fun for them, annoying and frustrating for me. I still blame devs for forcing this.

P.S. You don't need to buy Rise of the Angry Earth DLC anymore, it's included in the Standard Edition of NW: Aeternum.

review:
New World is very close to being a good game, but still isn't quite there.


When leveling the game is trying to balance three systems that are all competing for your attention:
Main story quests
Faction quests
Trade skills

The problem with this balance is that if you interact with two of them, your level outpaces the content they provide. Not only that, but your future progression is locked behind them AND artificial time gates. If you target your faction quests in order to buy your roughly third best armor. You'll reach a point where it tells you to travel into the Elysian Wilds, so you go to the Elysian Wilds and a menu pops up saying you can't travel into the Elysian Wilds because you haven't done the Elysian Wilds story quest. You pull up your map and you may have 3 separate main story quests at this point, The one you've been progressing throughout your time playing the game, the one for the other starting area you didn't spawn at, and the main story quest for the heartrune item slot. Oh rats, the big flashing quest the game told you was important when you unlocked it was the wrong thing to focus on and you need to wait to do it.

Now you have a 25% chance that the expedition you want to run is in the current mutator rotation if not you can either work on your trade skills for tens or hundreds of hours to maybe even skip a step in the gear ladder, check the trading post to buy it outright, or you could run possibly up to a second level mutation of one of the dungeons currently in rotation, and assuming you run every dungeon you're allowed to that week with the highest grade you can get, you'll be able to make two pieces you're looking for, also you might need to re-roll it's third perk which is a 3 day wait for the materials (or a 1/week run through the Hive of Gorgons.) and it's a bit costly too but hey it might be your best in slot gear. After that, you have nothing material to work towards so of course the developers need to inflate the play time.


Dear developers, the endgame needs a major overhaul, even if it's as simple as being able to group with 5 people and participate in mutated variants of dungeons outside of the queued rotation to actually let your players work toward the content they want. 

After that, let them add more mutations past the 3 mutation cap just to test and play around. Don't limit the avenues players can take to try to enjoy your game.

New World feels like a passion project plagued with shortcuts to release the game looking completed before it was ready.

review:
New World is an amazing game with a handful of problems that are constantly being addressed. I just think they're addressing them and not, maybe, taking it to it's fullest depth. I had written a lengthy review. I'll try to post elsewhere for the devs to see. I get pretty specific there but I'll summarize for ya'll. 

Right now, endgame boils down to repetitive loops: run Myrk, run world bosses, run raids, do the same dungeons, grind OPR or 3s, repeat. It's all fun (especially the world bosses and PVP), but it's thin. When M1 gear is being salvaged or sold, and even M2 gear often doesn’t stick, something's off.

Want longevity? Make endgame revolve around unlocking quests with multi-faceted requirements. Add unique rewards that show off effort, not just RNG luck. Create progression where gathering, crafting, and skill investment matter. Including adding a profession system as I mentioned earlier. Professions and Crafting should go with the quests like PB&J.

Brimstone Sands and the Heartrune quest line were steps in the right direction. Players had to be a certain level, finish story lines, and work toward something meaningful. Keep that energy but go deeper.

The early player complaints about slow crafting/gathering leveling? That was a good feature. Progress should be hard. It should feel earned. Nowadays, we level way too fast. Maxing out gathering/crafting skills is normalized, not revered. Bring back that sense of accomplishment.

And most importantly, Questing. 

New World’s quests mostly boil down to "go here, kill this, grab that." Even in zones like Cutlass Keys, the rewards are disproportionately low. If it takes me 15 minutes to complete a quest for 35 doubloons, that isn’t rewarding. It’s discouraging. Though I do recognize that some of the newer quests are actually really really well done (having to make that pot to go into the Elysian Wilds was a really nice touch) and I think AGS is onto something.

Still, compare this to a game like RuneScape. Quests like While Guthix Sleeps demand high-level skill investment, prior quest completions, and real player agency. There are puzzles, investigations, cinematic lore reveals, and progression gated behind your achievements as a player. You're not just killing something. You're becoming something.

You’ve built something really special here, AGS. But if players can reach max level in 20 hours, burn out on the same 4 loops, and see little reason to return until the next season, the system needs tweaking.

Focus on adventure, make quests memorable, and make effort visible. Let the endgame be something players spend years working toward. 

You've got lightning in a bottle with New World. Just give it a better bottle.

anonymous negative review:

New World is Amazon’s bold attempt to make a fantasy MMO… which mostly succeeds in reminding you why two-handed axes and global trade systems should never be designed by the same people who sell you bulk cat litter.

You start off shipwrecked on Aeternum, a mysterious island full of magic, monsters, and 700 players all trying to skin the same boar. Your mission? Unclear. Something about corruption, ancient secrets, and chopping down enough trees to personally cause fantasy climate change.

The combat is action-based, which is cool… until you realize it’s just dodge-roll, light attack, heavy attack, repeat. PvE feels like whacking angry scarecrows with a wet baguette, while PvP is either a sweaty arena of backflipping murder-hobos or a 50v50 lag-fest where your sword swings five seconds after you press the button and then your character dies of confusion.

The quests? Oh, they’re rich—in copy and paste. Every town needs you to:

Kill 12 skeletons.

Collect 10 wolf pelts.

Run back and forth between the same three huts like a medieval DoorDash driver.

After 40 hours of this, you’ll start to question if you’re the hero, or just the world's most overqualified exterminator.

And don’t even get me started on the economy. At launch, it was so broken people were using furniture to duplicate gold and destabilize the economy like fantasy hedge fund managers. Now it’s stabilized, meaning you can finally sell 200 iron ingots for... 3 coins and a handshake.

Crafting and gathering are oddly satisfying at first. You’ll spend hours cutting trees, mining ore, and skinning animals… until you realize you’re playing Lumberjack Simulator Online and haven't actually fought an enemy in three real-world days. But hey—your logging skill is maxed, so that’s something.

Faction wars are hyped as epic battles for territory. In practice? It’s a bunch of color-coded players in matching cloaks trying to take over a point while frantically shouting in voice chat and getting wiped by a group named “YeetFleet.”

Conclusion:
New World has beautiful visuals, a promising world, and a crafting system that could power three MMOs on its own. But after the novelty wears off, you’re left with repetitive quests, shallow endgame, and the creeping realization that you’ve been running back and forth between the same two towns for 10 hours just to deliver cabbage.

review:
Disclaimer: I didn't really start playing this game until Season 3 or 4, when a lot of things had already been fixed with the game.

I'll start with the good:
-The combat is amazing! The attacks, blocks, dodging is incredibly smooth and extremely satisfying!
-This was my first MMO, and I had a blast figuring out how to play a Tank role, pulling large groups of mobs and using my threat to keep aggro while my DPS go to town.
-There is a lot of depth to the game if you are new to MMO's: Figuring out how to maximize your Damage, how to maximize your Fortify, how to maximize your Healing, etc.
-I took my time with the storyline, and did most of my own experimentation: I made my own builds and had a ton of fun learning on my own. I highly recommend doing this yourself, don't just watch a Youtube video and bypass 75% of the game to get a 'perfected' endgame build. The fun is in the journey! Not the destination.
-The gathering is also extremely satisfying. I did nearly ALL my own gathering for my first playthrough and really enjoyed it: Finding a route with a good amount of the resources that I wanted that wasn't heavily camped. You can even get outfits to maximize your gathering yield while you're out there!
-The new-and-improved Expedition system is fantastic! It makes it simple and easy to get into fast matches, and if you queue for random expeditions, you get a reward for your first three! A great, fun source of daily money!

Now for the bad:
-There are a lot of bugs in the game. I didn't really start noticing them until I got to end-game. To their credit, the devs have dealt with a large portion of them, but (in my opinion) they take too long to address them.
Example: The MAIN raid, Hive of Gorgons, has some complex mechanics at the last boss fight. There was a bug that made nearly all the mechanics INVISIBLE during the entire fight - And this happened pretty much 100% of the time. This was reported to have started in January 2025. The devs "fixed" the issue in April (THREE WHOLE MONTHS) and their "fix" didn't improve things AT ALL.
I honestly can't remember when it was FINALLY fixed, I think sometime in May or June. But this is their MAIN content - What people play THE MOST, and it took them 5+ MONTHS to fix a MAJOR issue with it.

So my point is: if you play New World, be prepared to encounter annoying bugs in the game that won't be fixed anytime soon.

-The game also goes through content droughts. The devs release a new Season ~every 3 months, but a lot of the different Seasons are snoozers. If you're new, the events and rewards will be exciting and extremely fun, but most of the playerbase has seen these events for the better part of 3 or 4 years now, and there isn't much incentive for older players to come back and do them again.

I, personally, wholeheartedly recommend this game to players who haven't played an MMO before and who have a group of friends to play this with. This game has become my most-played game on Steam, and I have enjoyed every moment of it! I've met some awesome people, and even met some of them in real-life. It has been a truly life-changing experience for me, and for the better.
But if you're a hardened MMO veteran, there probably isn't much to this game that you haven't seen already. Unless you're interested in trying it out for yourself, I think a lot of MMO's play better than this one, and have a larger player base.

I got a solid 1,000 to 2,000 hours out of this game before I could say I mastered the different aspects of it, like healing, DPS'ing and tanking. I had a ton of fun learning about all the mechanics, how to play the raid, how to do all the different expeditions, etc.
I'm not a PvP person, so I didn't really touch that side of things, except for the few games I played of Outpost Rush in order to grind my PvP track. (NOT a fan of that, btw. I don't agree with forcing people to do content they hate in order to get something they want)

But I definitely recommend this game! To me, it's worth playing, even with the annoying bugs, the occasional empty Seasonal content, the issues that take months to resolve, everything.
At the end of the day, it's an extremely satisfying MMO that I hope to come back to again and again!

review:
Yesterday I would've said this game is, though not the best, reasonably good. Today I think it's incredibly poorly designed to the point that were i not playing exclusively to play with my friends, I'd be dropping it entirely at this point. 

I came back to the game recently having previously played an older version of it a year or two ago. With everything that's happened I was told it'd be best to start over on a new character so that's what I did. I enjoyed most of the story questing - although it's a little tedious at times, parts of it felt well-written and reasonably engaging. I realize the writing isn't really why people play it but in a game that has quests that's important to me. 

Recently I hit lvl 60 and today I started at lvl 62. Me and my friend had been doing faction missions off and on since we realized the faction gear would be our best for now, and so were incentivized to hit peak faction rank. It's not a grind i particularly enjoy but I've played other grindy games and I had done this before on my old account, so it was bearable.

We get the points needed to start the final faction quest, completion of which is required to buy max-level faction gear - the only requirement stated is that it *recommends* level 65. Well, I'm 62 so that's probably close enough to get through the combat right? So I go to talk to the npc....and I can't start the quest. Even though I have all the stated requirements for it, and lvl 65 is just a recommendation, according to the people who wrote it. Whatever, I guess I'll go back to main story for a while. 

I go back to main story quests and hit lvl 64. 64 is the level required to buy and equip the highest-level faction gear. Again, the game does not state that you need to be lvl 64 to do the faction quest, only that it suggests that you be level 65. Still, we decide to go try to pick up the faction mission again because if 65 is a hard requirement even though the gear is 64 that's a whole other problem. Well good news, it let me pick up the quest! Bad news, it wouldn't let me until I was 64! That means level 64 is a hard requirement even though this isn't stated in the requirements for the quest!

Regardless, we're just glad to be getting on with it so get on with it we do. We go kill two of the bosses we need, and there's a third yet to fight...in Elysian fields. 

The faction quest which stated no requirements, and only had a suggested criteria of lvl 65, ACTUALLY requires that you be lvl 64 AND have main story completed. Nowhere is this stated. If we hadn't guessed that maybe the level requirement was higher I would've wondered if my game was bugged, *because the game doesn't even tell you what the actual requirements are*. 

SO I GUESS WE'RE GOING BACK TO THE MAIN STORY TO UNLOCK ELYSIAN FIELDS!

Compared to the earlier quests, the writing in the lategame feels weak and rushed. Again, I realize the writing isn't what people are playing for but it's sad that it feels like they just stopped caring about their own story. It devolves into a series of fetchquests and a tour of some of the northern regions for no particular reason. We get towards what seems to be the concluding fight, and Grace O'Malley - a character you meet at the start - shows up and just Mary-Sue's some guy in one hit? The same chick that spent 6 hours trying to solve a puzzle that takes 5 minutes? And who had gotten on a ship to dive into a storm? It felt very hamfisted and like pandering for something that no one would want to be pandered for. WHY ARE YOU HERE? AND WHY DO YOU MAGICALLY NOT SUCK AFTER BEING USELESS ALL GAME?

But whatever, it's time to kill Isabella!

Oh my god. Isabella. I would drop the game here and now if I hadn't made a promise to raid with my friend in the post-story game. 

Over half of the Isabella fight is her being untargetable. This is not due to shielding, or some mechanic where you need to break her immunity, or any other logical reason. She just spontaneously becomes immune mid-swing *for the sake of monolouging and looking pretty in a cutscene*. THE WHOLE ENTIRE FIGHT IS A GLORIFIED CUTSCENE IN WHICH THE BIG BAD SPENDS HALF OF IT IMMUNE. She's standing still and not attacking me? Too bad, I can't hit her, or her minions. Nevermind that I'm a dps WHOS ENTIRE GOAL IN THIS FIGHT is to take the enemy down as fast as I can and I'm alone, making this a top priority. Instead she's constantly becoming immune, then stopping to monologue, then swinging at me 3 times before becoming immune again, and then theres a 20 second cutscene where I'm immobolized. 

Then, the """fight""" resumes (because is it even a fight if my spear goes right through her doing nothing with 0 indicators or mechanics involved?) and I get hit once and die from full health, even despite dodging her attacks at every turn possible. 

After some troubleshooting, we discovered I was dying to the floor. The floor was near-instantly killing me in the late phase of the fight. The way to mitigate this is by buying and drinking a potion that has not been mentioned or used at any point before or up to this fight. Drank it and died in one hit at that same phase anyway, that time might have been my mistake but at this point its almost impossible to tell. Still haven't beaten her and I've half a mind to leave the game over this. 

I had been enjoying the game up to this point but between the poor quest requirement implementation and how downright infuriating this storyline fight has been I cannot say that the game is well designed. Because it is not. None of this is good game design. Yes, the final fight is difficult, and I enjoy the ways in which it is difficult...so why am I not allowed to engage with the fight? Why did a faction quest require lategame main story completion but did not say as much as a requirement? Why were the level requirements for starting the quest not stated? Why can't I do the quest and just not be allowed to buy the gear? IS IT BECAUSE OF THE MAIN STORY REQUIREMENT? BECAUSE YOU DON'T STATE THAT ANYWHERE!

I'll probably try the fight again tomorrow and get through it at some point and have a Perfectly Okay time in the post-story raids and other pvm shenanigans. I don't care. That doesn't to me make this game any better. If you're going to try to make me care about the gameplay then make the gameplay worth caring about.

review:
Short Version:
The game is fun with friends but suffers from fast leveling, repetitive gear farming, limited PvP, and seasonal servers that only split the player base without real rewards.

Full Version:
First off, the game is incredibly fun when playing with friends — one of whom actually gifted it to me — which really adds to the enjoyment. However, it definitely has its flaws.

While there’s now more to do in the game than at launch, most of these activities take far less time to complete. The developers have made leveling up too easy, and it now happens so quickly that it feels empty rather than rewarding. Reaching max level doesn’t feel like an achievement anymore; instead, it’s just the point where the real grind actually begins — farming the best bosses for the BIS gear you really want.

Crafting your own weapons and armor usually isn’t worth it either. Found gear often has unique perk combinations that crafting simply can’t replicate, so the only real path to top-tier equipment is farming the hardest bosses over and over. But once you finally have your BIS setup, there’s no real reason to keep doing PvE, since it stops being challenging or rewarding altogether.

Once you reach BIS levels, PvP ends up being the only real option left, but it often feels forced rather than natural. There are really only two PvP modes: a dedicated game mode, where most of the actual PvP activity happens, and open-world PvP within the normal map — either in special PvP areas or through random encounters while flagged. This makes the endgame feel surprisingly shallow. There’s a lot on offer, but once you’re fully geared, there’s not much real incentive to do any of it.

Seasonal servers have now been introduced, but this feels like it only splits the player base without offering any major rewards or benefits to either group.

review:
I really wanted to love this game.
I remember the hype, the trailers, the idea of a new MMO that could finally break the mold — something fresh, something exciting.

And for a few hours... it was exciting.
The world is beautiful, the combat feels responsive, and the soundtrack hits just right. But after that?
It’s like a beautiful shell with nothing inside.

The grind is unbearable.
Not the fun kind of grind where you feel rewarded after hours — I’m talking about repetitive, copy-paste quests like "kill 10 of these" and "gather 5 of those"... over and over.
And the worst part? Most of them send you running across the map for 15 minutes just to collect something that takes 30 seconds.

The economy? Broken.
Crafting felt meaningful at first — until you realize that everyone’s crafting the same gear and undercutting each other.
Gold inflation, useless items, and towns that can’t even be maintained because players stop caring after a while.

PvP?
Fun for a bit, until you realize how much of it is dominated by zergs, exploits, and imbalance.
If you're solo or casual, forget about being competitive.

But what really broke it for me wasn’t the bugs, the lag, or even the bots.
It was this lingering feeling of emptiness.
Like you're grinding and grinding... for what?
The story is forgettable, the world doesn’t evolve, and after a while, you just feel like you’re playing out of habit, not enjoyment.

I kept telling myself,

“It’ll get better with the next patch.”
“The devs are listening.”
“Maybe next content drop will fix it.”

But weeks turned into months, and I just stopped logging in.

Is it the worst MMO out there?
No.
But it’s a reminder that pretty graphics and good mechanics mean nothing if the soul isn’t there.
I didn’t quit because it was hard.
I quit because it was empty.

review:
Here is a pros and cons review at level 37, for people who are considering purchasing the game on sale. Starting with negatives. I will go directly to the points.

-Boring, repetitive quests. Questing is basically opening containers, killing x amount of enemies, talking to NPCs. Nothing creative, nothing fun. Old azz boring MMO questing for a “modern” MMO. Very poor choice of design.

-Ordinary story for the main quest line, not interesting at all. While I am questing, I try to listen to conversations and read the things I find in general. But for this game, I skip everything. It is just to keep the player busy before the repetitive “go open that many containers” quests.

-Kept mounts behind DLC for old players. This game is a torture without mounts, and I cannot believe that they made people play this game without mounts for around 3 years! What a poor design choice. It is not surprising that 90 percent of their player base stopped playing.

-Boring fishing.

-Repetitive music.

-Includes game pass. (I hate game pass in games!)

So why did I give this game a thumbs up after all? Here are the pros:

+Simple action combat. No generic, old-school, and boring MMO combat. You have two weapons, and each weapon has 3 skills of your choice from 6 alternatives. That's all. Very simple and enjoyable. Definitely, less is more.

+Easily resettable weapon and general skill system that does not force you into one kind of play style.

+Side quests are located near and related with main quests generally.

+Joining a faction, and doing faction quests make it easier to reach higher quality items and gathering & crafting XP's.

+Player-friendly storage, gathering, and crafting system. Everything is very simple and enjoyable; no exaggerated, complex, time-wasting crafting. Enjoyable, easy, and you will acquire quality items at the end.

+Player-driven economy. You can sell and purchase items directly from the trade-post, or craft, try to acquire items from quests.

+Beautiful game atmosphere.

This is not a modern game if you remove combat and crafting. Still, it is probably one of the most enjoyable action combat MMOs out there and includes fun stuff. There are tons of things to do.  If you like this kind of combat, this game promises some. I haven’t even tried open world PvP, end-game, dungeons, or raids yet.

P.S. I saw some complaints about the population not being enough for an MMO in general. My starting server is populated enough and does not feel abandoned at all. Also you cannot see real player number in Steam, because the servers are cross-platform. Additionally, since gathering a node makes it disappear, I prefer fewer players lol. But still there are players everywhere when questing etc. It does not matter really if there are 5k, 10k or 50k players total.

review:
Beautiful but Broken: A Stunning MMO Undone by Its Own Systems

At first glance, this game is breathtaking. The visual quality is top-tier – environments are richly detailed, and I have to give special praise to the dungeon design. The atmosphere, lighting, and visual storytelling in those areas truly blew me away while exploring the game for the first time. It felt like there was something magical here – something worth investing time in.

And yet, as I reached the later stages of the game, that initial wonder began to fade. What replaced it was something much less enchanting: a system built around grind, RNG, and what feels like a casino-inspired loot loop.

Inventory Hell
Let’s start with the biggest flaw: the inventory system. It's a mess. You spend an absurd amount of time just sorting through endless piles of junk – useless armor, weapons, and trinkets that serve no purpose. There's no satisfying way to sell or discard them. It’s not just clutter; it actively kills momentum and enjoyment. In WoW, even bad loot had a reason to exist. Here, it’s just digital garbage.

Combat and Progression
The combat is actually good – smooth, responsive, and enjoyable. But the progression is bizarrely lopsided. Leveling is way too fast and easy, while gathering professions like mining become a painful, drawn-out grind. It feels like two separate games – one rushing you forward, the other dragging you back.

Disconnected World, Shallow Exploration
Despite the beautiful locations, the world feels oddly disconnected. There's no meaningful interaction with the environment, no real sense of presence. You don’t need to explore, and once you've seen an area, there’s little reason to return. The world is too small, too static. New zones should be arriving yearly, along with a steady flow of new dungeons and raids – not just recycled ones with increased difficulty.

From Immersion to Slot Machines
This is where the real disappointment hits. The game slowly shifts from immersive MMO to something that feels designed around loot crate addiction. The gameplay ends up revolving around opening boxes, hoping for a lucky drop – like a slot machine in a 24/7 convenience store. That kind of design breaks the fantasy, breaks the immersion, and ultimately breaks the game.

Economy in Chaos
The auction house is another weak link. Because of the nonsensical item system, prices are wildly inconsistent. It’s difficult to judge value, and trading becomes more frustrating than rewarding. It’s a symptom of the game’s deeper design issues.

Bright Spots Still Exist
To be fair, there are elements worth celebrating. The voice-acted NPC dialogue during story quests is a huge plus. Hearing characters speak adds a layer of immersion and personality that plain text just can’t deliver – and it genuinely made me care more about the main story, at least at first. More MMOs should do this.

World bosses and live events also shine – for brief moments, you feel part of a living, breathing community. And the musical instruments and group performances? Pure genius. These systems are fun, original, and show a glimpse of the game’s untapped potential.

Conclusion: A Lost Opportunity
This game could have been one of the greats. It had the budget, the engine, the setting. For a while, it looked like it might truly rival the giants of the genre. But over time, poor design choices, inventory frustration, and a shift toward “casino-style” systems have dragged it down.

It’s beautiful, but broken. A haunting reminder of how potential means nothing without vision.

review:
I am perplexed by the hate in the reviews. I've noticed alot of times lately games become 'popular to hate' when they have a launch that is flawed in any way, or even just not the end-all-be-all game to spend every future waking second playing for them personally, they start or create some kind of hate train.

As a traditional fantasy MMORPG format, this is one of the newest and by far the best iterations of that genre. This game has one of the best combat systems ever put in an MMORPG, BY FAR. With active, split second dodging, real hit-boxes where you can jump over and duck under projectiles and swings actually miss if they don't physically touch you. I believe there are character collisions as well, IIRC. All projectiles have to actually be aimed, which adds a HUGELY immersive element to large raids or the fortress defense activity things. For instance, as an archer, you are actually aiming the arrows slightly upward to compensate for gravity's pull, so the arrows fall into the mob of melee fighting going on ahead of you between the enemy NPC melee and your own RAID group. Combat is fast paced, and positioning matters greatly, ESPECIALLY when using a weapon like rapier. Every fraction of a second matters because some of your abilities effectively teleport behind the enemy, but doesn't stun for like 3 seconds like in WOW. You are just using your abilities and positioning to actually physically dodge the enemies attacks. Not getting hit no matter what, and hoping it rolls well, again, like in traditional MMORPGs. The combat in this is much faster paced and way more movement, positioning, and timing involved because you actually have to 'HIT' the enemy, and they you.

The class system is great; you can effectively level every class on one character if you choose, and the same goes for crafting/skills type leveling. 

The music system is bar-none the absolute best. The game practically has Guitar Hero (without the guitar controls, so step mania?) or Rockband just built into the game as a skill to level and progress. And you can do it with your other party members or whomever, and each person plays a different instrument and part of the song.. for like 100s of songs, IIRC.

The builds system is unique and very customizable. Each weapon has a major and minor stat that contributes to it. And you can equip two weapon types to switch between. So, I.E. speccing with high dexterity helps you as a 'major' stat for both bow and spear. But, it also helps by contributing half points to things like Hatchet and Two handed sword as a 'Minor' stat. combine this with magic type weapons, and a talent tree style system, and you get the picture. 

Sorry if some of it is vague, a lot is coming from memory. But I am actually reinstalling the game right now.

One tip: Check the server populations online before you make your character. Currently, in the US, Us West servers are virtually empty compared to the healthy population on Us East. XD

Anyways, if you're looking for a traditional(ish) fantasy MMORPG with great combat and leveling and skills system.... New World is actually my 10/10 favorite.

I want my character to look cool but damn if it's going to cost that much I'd rather pay a sub and have it thrown in for free.

Overall, 7/10

review:
TLDR: Fun earlygame but even before reaching the end of Main Story line it becomes very repetitive and boring. Needs more variety when it comes to combat and content.

Story is decent, although has a few dips here and there (IMO first big bad introduction as corrupting cunning force was pretty weak, she seemed like a 100% villain with taunts rather than making valid points). Sidequests range from normal to a bit weird, but almost all are voiced. They do lack variety though, there aren't really any proper puzzles or custom mechanics tied to quests like in some other MMOs.

The world is pretty but looting broken houses for absolutely the same materials gets quite repetitive very fast. The game really would benefits from metas and dynamic world events that some other MMOs have.

Combat is a mixed experience. From one point of view it's very responsive. From another it's just switching between 2 weapons with 3 active skills of out 6 toal + very minor skill customization. Oh and also +1 skill from heartrune. It lacks depth, variety. Feels spammy and by the time I reached Elysian Wilds I got bored with it, even though I started switching ranged weapon between bow and firestaff.
On top of that DPS builds are too squishy. It's not fun when enemy sneezes at you and you lose 50% hp or straight up get oneshot.
Blocking is very hard because of visual spam, it's just impossible to see when enemies attack. And there is no option to turn down/hide ally skill effects, so if you're part of 20-man raid, the screen is a multicolored vomit.

I didn't quite get into endgame content aside from trying some open world elite chest runs and M1 expeditions, but it seems that endgame is mostly raid and mutated expedition grind. review:
The thing is, I saw some new vids on youtube and was like hell yeah let me revisit New World, you know, Amazon's flagship MMORPG, or as I like to call it, Jeff Bezos’ $500 million Minecraft server for bored spreadsheet enjoyers. If this game is the future of gaming, then grab your loincloth and stone tools, because we’re going back to the Dark Ages. Not the fun, sword-swinging Dark Ages the ones with lice, mud, and dysentery.

This game is less “New World” and more like “Expired Product Left in Bezos’ Garage Since 2018.” You log in, greeted by a loading screen (on my new killer rig with suck yo dack nvmes and shit) that lasts longer than Amazon’s commitment to workers’ rights, and enter a world where every single player is either a tree-chopping automaton or a shirtless gremlin spawn-camping a wolf den for crafting mats. You’re not building a fantasy empire you’re doing unpaid labor in a digital Amazon warehouse.

Fighting is is a mix of circle jerk and pray with all the satisfying impact of hitting a wiffle ball with a wet sock. Somehow, despite this being 2025, swordfighting feels like two mannequins slap-fighting  in a 2004 Dr. Who episode.   PVP boils down to what I call... the dance.   Moving on.
The story, which is like someone asked ChatGPT to write a fantasy plot but trained it exclusively on Amazon Prime TV scripts. You’ve got your usual “ancient evil,” “corrupted magic,” and “you are the chosen one” tropes, but written with all the depth of a Jeff Bezos LinkedIn post. The voice acting is a buffet of accents nobody asked for. One guy sounds like a Narubian pirate that has never seen the ocean, another like he’s doing a low-budget Bridgerton audition on syrup. I half-expected someone to say, “By the light of the Amazon Algorithm, Bezo's protects!”

Oh yeah the algorithms, i mean... auction house.  The game’s economy is a lawless stock market simulator run by dupe fiends who majored in meme coins. Inflation runs wild. A stick costs more than your first car. Gold farming is more lucrative than your actual job. Crafting is a Kafkaesque nightmare requiring 900 bear pelts, three star-metal penile implants, and the blood of Bezos himself to make a Level 3 chair.

The true glory here though, what really makes New World special is its glorious commitment to soulless bloat. Everything takes forever. Walk for 15 minutes, fight a boar, get 2 XP, repeat until you are dead inside. Bruh, I have played F2P Korean MMOs with more forgiving grinds.

Good News... the servers work.. Atlieast when I played again they did. Also it looks kind of nice most of the time.  Thats good I guess.
